chapter_title: Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) and Host-based Security
chapter_summary:
Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) are critical components of a comprehensive security strategy, designed to monitor network or system activities for malicious activity or policy violations. They don't prevent attacks directly but alert administrators to potential intrusions, allowing for timely response. We distinguish between Network-based IDS (NIDS), which monitor network traffic, and Host-based IDS (HIDS), which monitor individual systems. For LFCE, a strong focus on HIDS is essential, as it provides deep insight into the internal state of a server. Tools like OSSEC (Open Source Security Event Correlator) and AIDE (Advanced Intrusion Detection Environment) are prominent examples of HIDS. OSSEC is a powerful, open-source HIDS that performs log analysis, file integrity checking, rootkit detection, time-based alerting, and active response. AIDE, on the other hand, is primarily focused on file integrity monitoring (FIM).

File Integrity Monitoring (FIM) is a core function of HIDS, crucial for detecting unauthorized changes to critical system files, binaries, and configuration files. Attackers often modify these files to establish persistence, hide their tracks, or alter system behavior. AIDE works by creating a cryptographic hash (a "snapshot" or "baseline") of selected files and directories. You initialize the database with `sudo aide --init`, which creates a file like `/var/lib/aide/aide.db.new.gz`. After reviewing and moving it to `/var/lib/aide/aide.db.gz`, you can then regularly run `sudo aide --check` to compare the current state of files against this baseline. Any discrepancies (changes in size, permissions, hashes, etc.) are reported. It's vital to protect the AIDE database itself, typically by storing it on read-only media or in a secure, off-host location. A common mistake is to store the database on the same compromised filesystem, rendering it useless if an attacker modifies it. AIDE configuration is managed in `/etc/aide/aide.conf`, where you define which files/directories to monitor and what attributes to check (e.g., `p` for permissions, `i` for inode, `n` for number of links, `u` for user, `g` for group, `s` for size, `m` for mtime, `c` for ctime, `a` for atime, `md5` or `sha256` for file hashes). Schedule AIDE checks via `cron` and ensure reports are sent to a secure logging server or email address.

OSSEC offers a more comprehensive HIDS solution. It not only performs FIM but also provides real-time log analysis, rootkit detection, and active response capabilities. OSSEC agents are installed on monitored hosts and report to a central OSSEC manager. The manager then analyzes the collected logs and FIM data, correlating events and generating alerts based on predefined rules. For example, OSSEC can detect multiple failed SSH login attempts, changes to `/etc/passwd`, or the creation of suspicious SUID binaries. Its active response feature can automatically block an IP address via the firewall after a certain number of failed logins. Configuring OSSEC involves defining rules in XML files (e.g., `/var/ossec/etc/ossec.conf` and rules in `/var/ossec/etc/rules/`). For FIM, you specify directories to monitor (`<directories check_all="yes">/etc</directories>`). For log analysis, you define log files to ingest (`<localfile name="sshd" logfile="/var/log/auth.log"/>`). While powerful, OSSEC requires careful tuning to avoid alert fatigue and ensure relevant events are prioritized.

Network-based IDS (NIDS) like Snort or Suricata monitor network traffic in real-time for signatures of known attacks, policy violations, or anomalous behavior. While LFCE focuses more on host-based security, understanding NIDS principles is beneficial. Snort operates by applying a set of rules against incoming packets. A basic Snort rule consists of a rule header (action, protocol, source IP/port, direction, destination IP/port) and rule options (message, content match, flow, etc.). For example, `alert tcp any any -> $HOME_NET 21 (msg:"FTP Brute Force Attempt"; flow:to_server,established; content:"USER"; depth:4; threshold:type limit,track by_src,count 5,seconds 60; sid:1000001; rev:1;)` alerts on more than 5 FTP `USER` commands from the same source within 60 seconds. Deploying NIDS typically involves placing a sensor on a network segment where it can see all traffic (e.g., via a SPAN port or network tap). Analyzing NIDS alerts requires understanding network protocols and attack patterns. Integrating NIDS alerts with HIDS and centralized logging solutions provides a holistic view of the security landscape, enabling quicker detection and response to complex, multi-stage attacks.

screens.title: Intrusion Detection Systems and Host-based Security
screens.subtitle: Practical HIDS, FIM with AIDE, OSSEC agent basics, and NIDS fundamentals

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn why intrusion detection systems are essential to server security and how host-based tools give you visibility that network sensors can miss. We’ll emphasize practical HIDS work with AIDE for file integrity monitoring and OSSEC for combined log analysis, FIM, and active response. You will see concrete terminal commands for installing and initializing AIDE, how to configure OSSEC to monitor SSH and system directories, and the basic anatomy of a Snort rule so you can interpret NIDS alerts. This matters because attackers commonly change binaries, configuration files, or logs to persist or hide. File integrity monitoring detects those changes early, and log correlation identifies suspicious behavior patterns. By the end you will understand how HIDS and NIDS complement each other, how to protect your AIDE baseline, and how to tune rules to avoid alert fatigue. Think about a server that suddenly shows a new SUID binary and failed SSH attempts — these combined signals are what IDS monitoring is designed to surface and help you respond to quickly.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: HIDS and FIM provide deep host visibility; OSSEC extends that with log correlation and active responses, while NIDS like Snort add network-level context.

narration.text: This lesson prepares you to deploy and configure host-based intrusion detection tools and to implement file integrity monitoring so you can detect unauthorized changes to system files. First, you will deploy AIDE and understand how to create and protect a baseline of file hashes. The second objective is to configure OSSEC as a local agent to collect SSH logs and FIM events, which allows you to correlate actions and receive real-time alerts. Each objective focuses on practical commands and configuration lines you will use during the lab: package install commands, AIDE init and check, and OSSEC localfile and directories entries. You will learn not just the commands but also the rationale for each configuration choice, such as which directories to include or exclude and why the AIDE database must be stored off the monitored host. By practicing these steps, you build skills that let you detect tampering, suspicious logins, and file changes quickly and reliably.

narration.text: These objectives emphasize practical judgement: selecting file attributes to monitor, excluding noisy directories, and tuning alerts to avoid fatigue. You’ll practice editing /etc/aide/aide. conf to include attributes like permissions, inode, size, mtime, and strong hashes and to explicitly exclude non-critical volatile directories such as /var/log and /tmp. You will also practice tuning OSSEC rules and thresholds so that correlation rules trigger on real attacks, not normal system activity. The lab stresses that protecting the AIDE database is part of your security controls; storing it on the same writable filesystem invites an attacker to blind your FIM tool. Finally, you’ll interpret a Snort rule to recognize how network signatures and thresholds are expressed so you can map NIDS alerts to host events during an investigation. These judgement skills help you prioritize alerts and avoid false positives while preserving forensic integrity.

screens.title: What is an IDS? NIDS vs HIDS
screens.subtitle: Definition and practical roles in a monitoring strategy

narration.text: An Intrusion Detection System is a monitoring tool that observes system or network activity and raises alerts when it detects patterns that suggest malicious activity or policy violations. There are two broad forms: Network-based IDS monitors packets on the wire, looking for signatures or anomalous flows, while Host-based IDS runs on individual systems and inspects logs, file changes, and system artifacts. The practical difference matters: NIDS sees network context like packet payloads and scanning behavior but cannot see changes made locally to files or memory. HIDS provides deep insight into the internal state of a host — file hashes, permission changes, authentication logs, and rootkit indicators — which often reveals persistence and tampering that a network sensor cannot. A concrete example: if an attacker modifies /etc/passwd to add a backdoor account, AIDE or OSSEC on the host will detect the file change; a NIDS alone may not. A common misconception is that IDS prevents intrusions. IDSs generate alerts; they do not block traffic by default. Some HIDS solutions can perform active responses, but the primary value remains detection and timely response. Takeaway: use HIDS to detect integrity changes and NIDS to spot suspicious network activity, then correlate both for a complete picture.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: IDS monitors for malicious activity; HIDS inspects host internals and files while NIDS inspects network traffic.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › What is an IDS?
IDS Overview
An IDS observes activity and alerts on suspicious patterns; it does not guarantee prevention.
Network-based IDS (NIDS)
Monitors traffic for signatures or anomalies. Example: Snort inspects packets against rule signatures.
Host-based IDS (HIDS)
Monitors logs, file integrity, and host artifacts. Example: AIDE and OSSEC detect changed files and log events.
Concrete example
If /etc/passwd is modified, AIDE or OSSEC will report the change. A NIDS may only show the network activity that preceded the compromise, if any.
Common misconception
IDS does not inherently block attacks. HIDS may include active response features, but detection and proper investigation remain the primary outcomes.
Key Takeaway

Combine HIDS file checks with NIDS traffic monitoring and correlate alerts for stronger detection.

Check your understanding

Why would you still run a NIDS if you already have HIDS on all hosts?

screens.title: File Integrity Monitoring (FIM) with AIDE
screens.subtitle: How AIDE builds a baseline and detects changes

narration.text: File Integrity Monitoring validates that operating system and application files remain unchanged from an approved baseline. AIDE accomplishes this by computing cryptographic hashes and recording file attributes into a database snapshot, often called the baseline. When you initialize AIDE, it writes a database such as /var/lib/aide/aide. db. new. gz which you review and then move to /var/lib/aide/aide. db. gz. Subsequent checks compare the current file state to that baseline and report differences in attributes like size, permissions, owner, mtime, and hashes. A concrete example: you configure /etc and /usr/bin to be monitored with md5 and sha256 in /etc/aide/aide. conf; after initialization you create a test change like touching /etc/testfile. txt and run aide --check to see the new file reported. A key operational point is to exclude volatile directories such as /var/log and /tmp; failing to exclude them floods your reports with noise. Also, protect the AIDE database off-host or on read-only media to avoid an attacker simply overwriting your baseline — storing it on the same writable filesystem is a common fatal mistake. Reflect: which directories on your server should be monitored and which should be excluded?

keyIdea.title: FIM principle
keyIdea.text: AIDE captures a cryptographic baseline of files and attributes and reports deviations during checks.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › FIM with AIDE
How AIDE works
AIDE computes hashes and records attributes into a baseline database, then compares later to detect changes.
Attributes
Common options: p (permissions), i (inode), n (links), u (user), g (group), s (size), m (mtime), c (ctime), a (atime), md5, sha256.
Exclusions
Exclude /var/log, /tmp, /proc, /sys to avoid constant expected changes.
Key Takeaway

Baseline integrity plus careful exclusions are the core of reliable FIM.

Concrete terminal example
sudo apt update && sudo apt install aide aide-common
sudo aide --init
sudo mv /var/lib/aide/aide.db.new.gz /var/lib/aide/aide.db.gz
sudo aide --check
# To test: sudo touch /etc/testfile.txt then sudo aide --check
Tip: review the database file before moving it into /var/lib; keeping an offline copy prevents an attacker from erasing history.

narration.text: Installing and configuring AIDE is a short, repeatable process but one that requires attention to configuration choices. Start by installing the package for your distribution and then edit /etc/aide/aide. conf to define monitoring targets and attributes. A recommended set of monitored directories includes /boot, /etc, /bin, /sbin and /usr/bin, each with robust attributes and strong hashes like sha256. Explicitly add exclusions for volatile directories. After editing the config, initialize the database with aide --init, inspect the generated /var/lib/aide/aide. db. new. gz, then move it to /var/lib/aide/aide. db. gz to make it active. Schedule daily checks with cron to run aide --check and email results to root or send them to a central logging server for archival. A concrete example is provided in the lab: add monitoring lines for /etc and /usr/bin, run initialization, then simulate a change with touch and observe the reported diff. A common error is to accept every change by immediately running aide --update without investigating; instead, investigate alerts first and only update the baseline when changes are verified as legitimate. Installing and configuring AIDE means install, configure attributes and exclusions, initialize and secure the baseline, then schedule regular checks.. In practical terms, practical steps and configuration snippets. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Deployment process
keyIdea.text: Install, configure attributes and exclusions, initialize and secure the baseline, then schedule regular checks.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Installing AIDE
Step-by-step
  1. Install the package for your OS (apt or dnf).
  2. Edit /etc/aide/aide.conf to add directories with attributes and hashes.
  3. Exclude volatile directories (e.g., /var/log, /tmp).
  4. Run sudo aide --init and review the generated database.
  5. Move the database into place and schedule periodic checks via cron.
Do not accept changes blindly with aide --update; investigate alerts first.
Recommended config snippet
/etc    p+i+n+u+g+s+m+sha256
/usr/bin    p+i+n+u+g+s+m+sha256
/boot   p+i+n+u+g+s+m+sha256
!/var/log
!/tmp
!/proc
!/sys
After editing, initialize and move the database. Protect the stored database by copying it to read-only media or a separate secure host.

screens.title: Initialize and test AIDE baseline
screens.subtitle: Terminal demo: init, move DB, simulate a change, and check

narration.text: This walkthrough explains the exact terminal actions you perform when creating and verifying an AIDE baseline. Start by running the package installation if needed, then execute aide --init. That command scans configured paths and writes a new database file, commonly named /var/lib/aide/aide. db. new. gz. Before activating it, inspect its creation time and move it into the active location using sudo mv /var/lib/aide/aide. db. new. gz /var/lib/aide/aide. db. gz. Now simulate a file change for testing: create or modify a monitored file such as /etc/testfile. txt, then run sudo aide --check. The check output will list files that differ and which attributes changed. If you confirm the change is legitimate, update the baseline with sudo aide --update and again move the new database into place. A frequent operational mistake is keeping the database on the same writable filesystem; this allows an attacker to modify the DB and hide changes. Always keep an archived copy off-host or on read-only storage and review every alert before updating the baseline. Initialize and test AIDE baseline means initialize aide, move the new db to the active location, simulate a change, run aide --check, and investigate alerts before updating.. In practical terms, terminal demo: init, move db, simulate a change, and check. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Lab demo
keyIdea.text: Initialize AIDE, move the new DB to the active location, simulate a change, run aide --check, and investigate alerts before updating.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › AIDE Init & Test
Terminal commands
sudo apt update && sudo apt install aide aide-common
sudo aide --init
sudo mv /var/lib/aide/aide.db.new.gz /var/lib/aide/aide.db.gz
sudo aide --check
# Test: sudo touch /etc/testfile.txt
sudo aide --check
# If change is verified:
sudo aide --update
sudo mv /var/lib/aide/aide.db.new.gz /var/lib/aide/aide.db.gz
Inspect the output carefully. The check lists attribute differences so you can triage changes effectively.
Investigation checklist
  • Verify who changed the file and when from logs.
  • Check for related suspicious entries in auth and syslogs.
  • Do not update baseline until the change is validated.
  • Preserve the pre-change database copy offline for forensics.
If you see unexpected changes to core files like /etc/passwd, escalate and preserve evidence immediately.

screens.title: Protecting the AIDE database
screens.subtitle: Why the baseline’s storage matters and common mistakes

narration.text: The integrity of your AIDE baseline is as important as the checks themselves. If an attacker modifies the AIDE database file on the host, they can hide malicious changes by making the baseline reflect the new state. For that reason, you should never rely only on the host's writable filesystem for storing the canonical baseline. Practical protections include copying the baseline to read-only media, storing it on an external secure host, or keeping an archived copy in an immutable logging server. A common mistake is to initialize AIDE and leave the database only in /var/lib without additional protection. Another misstep is automatically updating the baseline on every check; this makes it easy to accept malicious changes. A proper workflow is to investigate alerts, confirm legitimate changes, then update and archive the new baseline. Example: after a verified package upgrade that modifies binaries, update AIDE on a controlled schedule and push the new baseline to a secure off-host archive. Always assume the host may be partially compromised and design baseline protection accordingly. Protecting the AIDE database means keep aide baselines off-host or read-only and never auto-accept changes without investigation.. In practical terms, why the baseline’s storage matters and common mistakes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Protect baselines
keyIdea.text: Keep AIDE baselines off-host or read-only and never auto-accept changes without investigation.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Protecting the AIDE DB
Threat model
If an attacker gains root, they can edit files and the AIDE database on the same filesystem, hiding their activity. Treat the baseline as sensitive forensic evidence.
Best practices
  • Copy baseline to read-only media or external host.
  • Archive historical baselines off-host.
  • Require manual validation before updating the baseline.
Operational pattern
  1. Init baseline and copy to secure archive.
  2. Run daily checks and review diffs.
  3. Investigate before updating baseline.
  4. Store updated baseline off-host after validation.
Protecting the baseline preserves your ability to detect attackers who attempt to erase their tracks.

screens.title: OSSEC overview: agents, manager, and active response
screens.subtitle: What OSSEC provides beyond FIM

narration.text: OSSEC is an open-source host-based IDS that extends file integrity monitoring with log analysis, rootkit detection, and active response. The typical deployment involves OSSEC agents on monitored hosts and an OSSEC manager that aggregates and analyzes events. Agents collect logs, perform FIM, and send events to the manager, which applies XML-defined rules to generate alerts. A practical example: configure an agent to monitor /var/log/auth. log and the /etc directory. If the agent sees multiple failed SSH logins followed by a new SUID binary, the manager can correlate these events and raise a high-priority alert. OSSEC’s active response capability can automatically add a firewall rule to block a source IP after repeated failures, reducing attack surface while you investigate. However, active responses must be tuned carefully to avoid blocking legitimate traffic or generating too many automated changes. OSSEC requires rule tuning and thoughtful selection of monitored paths to avoid alert fatigue and to ensure high-value events are surfaced promptly. OSSEC overview: agents, manager, and active response means ossec combines fim, log analysis, and optional active responses to provide richer host-based detection and rapid mitigation.. In practical terms, what ossec provides beyond fim. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: OSSEC combines FIM, log analysis, and optional active responses to provide richer host-based detection and rapid mitigation.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › OSSEC Overview
Components
  • Agents: run on hosts, collect logs and FIM events.
  • Manager: aggregates events, applies rules, and generates alerts.
  • Active response: optional scripts to block IPs or take other actions.
Example detection
Multiple failed SSH attempts followed by a changed file in /etc can be correlated to indicate a compromise. OSSEC rules elevate correlated sequences above single-file or single-log events.
Active response benefit: automatic temporary firewall bans for repeated attackers. Misconfiguration risk: false positives can block legitimate users.

screens.title: Configure OSSEC agent for SSH and FIM
screens.subtitle: Key ossec.conf entries for local monitoring

narration.text: Configuring an OSSEC agent to monitor SSH logins and file integrity requires editing /var/ossec/etc/ossec. conf and adding localfile and directories entries. For log analysis, add a localfile element with syslog format and the path to your auth log; OSSEC will parse entries like failed password or accepted password and apply rules. For FIM, add directories entries with check_all enabled to watch /etc, /bin, and /sbin. After editing the configuration, start and enable the ossec-hids-agent service so it persists across reboots. A concrete local configuration example is shown in the lab: a entry pointing to /var/log/auth. log and entries for /etc, /bin, and /sbin with realtime reporting enabled. Observe alerts in /var/ossec/logs/alerts/alerts. log and verify FIM alerts by creating a test file in /etc. Remember to tune which directories are monitored and the reporting granularity to prevent excessive alerts. Configure OSSEC agent for SSH and FIM means add <localfile> entries for logs and <directories> entries for fim, then enable the agent and monitor alerts.log for events.. sudo systemctl start ossec-hids-agent

Config examples

screens.title: Testing OSSEC: FIM and SSH alerts
screens.subtitle: Generate events, view alerts.log, and interpret results

narration.text: Testing OSSEC confirms that your agent is collecting the intended data and that rules are firing as expected. After configuring localfile and directories entries, generate a file change inside a monitored directory such as /etc by creating /etc/ossec_test_file. txt; OSSEC should generate a FIM alert. For SSH monitoring, perform several failed SSH login attempts from another terminal or machine; OSSEC rules can be tuned to generate a brute-force alert after a threshold of failures. Use sudo tail -f /var/ossec/logs/alerts/alerts. log to watch alerts in real time. A concrete test sequence: create the test file, watch for a FIM alert, then attempt 3–5 failed SSH logins and observe a correlation or threshold-based alert. Misconception check: seeing many raw log entries does not equal an incident — correlation and context matter. If alerts are too noisy, tune rule thresholds, or limit monitored files to high-value paths. After validation, document the test results and adjust rules to balance detection with noise. Testing OSSEC: FIM and SSH alerts means create test events for fim and ssh, watch alerts.log, and tune rules to ensure meaningful alerts without excessive noise.. In practical terms, generate events, view alerts.log, and interpret results. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Testing OSSEC
Test steps
  1. Create a monitored test file: sudo touch /etc/ossec_test_file.txt
  2. Watch the alerts: sudo tail -f /var/ossec/logs/alerts/alerts.log
  3. Generate failed SSH logins from another terminal and observe correlation alerts.
Document alerts and adjust configuration to reduce false positives while preserving detection.
Alert example
# watch alerts live
sudo tail -f /var/ossec/logs/alerts/alerts.log
# Sample alert will show file change and originating agent name with details
If you get too many alerts, prioritize high-value paths and tune rules for aggregated events instead of single occurrences.

screens.title: Snort basics: NIDS and rule anatomy
screens.subtitle: Reading a Snort rule to interpret NIDS alerts

narration.text: Network-based IDS like Snort monitor packets for patterns that match known signatures or suspicious behavior. Understanding a Snort rule helps you map a network alert to host events. A basic Snort rule has a header and options. The header specifies action, protocol, source and destination addresses and ports, and direction. The options include a message and content matches or flow checks, and may include thresholds. For example, a rule that alerts on repeated FTP USER commands might look for the USER string and apply a threshold of five events from the same source within 60 seconds. Concrete example from the chapter: alert tcp any any -> $HOME_NET 21 (msg:"FTP Brute Force Attempt"; flow:to_server,established; content:"USER"; depth:4; threshold:type limit,track by_src,count 5,seconds 60; sid:1000001; rev:1;). Misconceptions to avoid: a Snort alert alone does not prove a host compromise. Combine NIDS alerts with HIDS evidence, such as changed files or suspicious logins, to build a stronger case for investigation. screens.title: Integrating HIDS and NIDS into a monitoring strategy
screens.subtitle: Correlating alerts and centralizing logs for faster response

narration.text: A robust monitoring strategy combines HIDS and NIDS signals into centralized logs and an alerting workflow so analysts can see correlated patterns. OSSEC agents produce FIM and log events, while NIDS sensors like Snort produce network alerts. Centralize both streams in a logging server or SIEM so you can pivot from a network alert to host evidence quickly. For example, a Snort FTP brute-force alert that coincides with OSSEC reports of new files in /usr/bin and failed SSH logins forms a stronger hypothesis of compromise than any single alert alone. Architecturally, deploy OSSEC agents on critical hosts, an OSSEC manager to aggregate and correlate, and NIDS sensors on strategic network segments (SPAN ports or taps). Configure forwarding of OSSEC and Snort alerts to your centralized logging server, and create correlation rules to raise higher-priority incidents when multiple sources align. A common mistake is to let raw alerts pile up without correlation; prioritization and playbooks convert alerts into actionable investigations. screens.title: Tuning and avoiding alert fatigue
screens.subtitle: Practical tips for rule tuning and prioritization

narration.text: Alert fatigue undermines detection. Too many low-value alerts cause missed incidents and wasted analyst time. For FIM, focus monitoring on high-value paths like /etc, /bin, and /sbin, and exclude volatile directories that change frequently. For OSSEC rules, prefer correlation rules that aggregate repeated events by source IP with thresholds rather than firing on every single failed login. For NIDS, apply content depth and flow options to reduce false positives. A concrete tuning example: use threshold or limit options to only alert after five failed attempts from the same IP within a minute. Document whitelists for known automated updates or maintenance windows so you do not generate noise for expected changes. Regularly review alert volumes and adjust rulesets; involve operations teams to understand scheduled changes so you can plan exclusions or maintenance modes. The key is to detect meaningful anomalies while preserving analyst attention for high-confidence alerts. screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.subtitle: Three core reminders from this chapter

narration.text: Three concise ideas to remember: First, a Host-based IDS (HIDS) like AIDE or OSSEC inspects host internals — files, permissions, and logs — and is essential for detecting tampering that network sensors cannot see. Second, File Integrity Monitoring works by creating a cryptographic baseline and comparing current files to it; protect that baseline off-host and do not update it without investigation. Third, OSSEC combines FIM with log analysis and can perform active response, but it requires careful tuning so automated actions do not cause outages. Keep these ideas in mind as operational rules: protect your evidence, correlate multiple signals before escalating, and tune alerts to remain actionable. screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 2
screens.subtitle: Three practical rules to apply immediately

narration.text: Three practical rules: First, always exclude noisy system paths from FIM to keep alerts useful. Second, never store the canonical AIDE database solely on the monitored host — archive it off-host or on read-only media. Third, tune OSSEC and NIDS rules to use thresholds and correlation, so you catch coordinated attacks rather than isolated log entries. These steps reduce false positives, preserve forensic integrity, and make alerts actionable. As you work through the lab, apply these rules and reflect after each test: did the alert tell you something you couldn’t have found otherwise? If not, tune and repeat.
